newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Lambsdorff says delay EMU if necessary.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Lambsdorff says delay EMU if necessary.

text.p: A former German economics minister told the weekly Stern that European monetary union (EMU) should be delayed if the necessary convergence criteria were not fulfilled, but that there was room for flexible interpretation.

Otto Lambsdorff, a leading member of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said the Maastricht treaty's government deficit target could be viewed more loosely than Bonn had chosen to do so far.
"Three point zero is wrong. There is some room to play with: not up to 3.5. But whether 3.2 or 3.3 -- we shall see," Lambsdorff told Stern, according to an advance release from Wednesday's edition.

The Maastricht treaty demands that government deficits do not overshoot three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), and Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly insisted that this means 3.0 percent and no more.
Few economists expect Bonn to meet this target in 1997, however.

Lambsdorff also said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's aim of cutting unemployment -- currently at a post-war record high of 4.7 million -- by 2000 was an illusion and said Kohl had been at the helm for too long for a parliamentary democracy.
He warned that the economic situation in Germany was so serious that Kohl's hopes for further European integration were in danger.
